claims.text: Dependency rule: no compile-time dependency points out of the code that holds the business rules; that code names only its own types and .NET's, never a class, package or project of the data access or web code around it.
claims.source_hint: glossary dependency-rule; outline item 4; .NET architecture guide, common web application architectures (Clean/Onion)

claims.text: In a classic layered design each layer depends on the one below it, so the business layer depends on the data-access layer and, through it, on the database technology; call and dependency arrows point the same way.

At stage-1 DonHang.Infrastructure.csproj has one ProjectReference, to ..\DonHang.Domain\DonHang.Domain.csproj (line 11); DonHang.Domain.csproj has no ItemGroup: no ProjectReference and no PackageReference.

OrderService (DonHang.Domain) takes IOrderRepository and INotifier; PlaceOrderAsync calls repository.AddAsync and SaveChangesAsync. IOrderRepository is declared in DonHang.Domain with four methods using only Order, List<Order>, int and Task.

EfOrderRepository (DonHang.Infrastructure) has using DonHang.Domain and using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore, implements IOrderRepository, returns Order, and queries db.Orders.Include(...) through DonHangDbContext.

When the API runs, dependency injection gives OrderService an EfOrderRepository behind IOrderRepository: ServiceCollectionExtensions registers services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>().

DonHang.Domain references no project and no package, so the compiler finds only its own types and those of the .NET framework it targets; naming EfOrderRepository or an EF Core type there fails the build.
claims.source_hint: .NET docs: ProjectReference/PackageReference; msbuild-props DisableTransitiveProjectReferences; local build CS0234

claims.text: At stage-1 no .cs file in DonHang.Domain names EfOrderRepository, DonHang.Infrastructure, EntityFrameworkCore or Npgsql.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-1: git grep -e EfOrderRepository -e DonHang.Infrastructure -e EntityFrameworkCore -- DonHang.Domain (no match)

claims.text: DonHang.Tests.csproj references DonHang.Domain (line 18); DonHang.Api.csproj references DonHang.Domain and DonHang.Infrastructure (lines 12-13).
At stage-1, `git grep -n "ProjectReference" -- "DonHang.*/*.csproj"` prints four lines: DonHang.Api.csproj:12 and :13, DonHang.Infrastructure.csproj:11, DonHang.Tests.csproj:18.
claims.source_hint: run in examples/don-hang at stage-1 (verified locally with git grep on the tag); git-grep docs, pathspec

claims.text: The dependency rule limits the direction of references, not their number; a reference between two projects outside the business rules (Api to Infrastructure) is not decided by this rule.
If IOrderRepository were declared in the data project next to its implementation, the business project would need a reference to the data project and, through it, to EF Core.
A ProjectReference is transitive by default in SDK-style projects: a project that references DonHang.Infrastructure also gets its package references (EF Core, Npgsql) and cannot build without them.
claims.source_hint: msbuild-props.md: DisableTransitiveProjectReferences (transitive by default); NuGet PackageReference transitive dependencies

claims.text: Removing the ProjectReference from DonHang.Infrastructure.csproj makes EfOrderRepository.cs fail to compile (CS0246) because IOrderRepository and Order can no longer be found.
